Reviews · Mazda Protegé5

The Happy Medium

Mazda built a hot sedan, then a turbocharged one, and in between it quietly built the best of the three. Twenty-plus years later the Protegé5 is the cheapest way left to buy a car that talks back.

By Oliver Bacon · 19 min read

This is, in a sense, a continuation of the MP3 story. It also very much deserves its own piece, because the Protegé5 is not a footnote to the sport-compact Mazdas on either side of it. It is the one that got the recipe right.

There is something about its size, its stance, its plucky demeanor. The whole car says I am fun and you will enjoy my company, and it says it before you have touched the door handle. It is like that kid at school who was always smiling and having a great time no matter what was in front of them — a brutal math test, a dodgeball game, a speech in front of the class. They did well. They enjoyed themselves. You were intrigued, and you knew that being around them would make your day better.

That is the Protegé5 in a nutshell. Always up for an adventure. You say hey, let's go here, or let's do this, and it answers with an enthusiastic grin: sounds awesome.

Where it sat in the family

To understand why the Protegé5 works, it helps to see the three cars Mazda built in a row.

First came the 2001 Protegé MP3, which arrived from a company that had just started saying zoom-zoom out loud and needed something on a showroom floor to back the claim up. Mazda took the ES sedan, had the Anaheim tuner Racing Beat work over the springs, dampers and anti-roll bars, recalibrated the ignition and intake for another 10 horsepower, bolted on 17-inch Racing Hart wheels, and filled the trunk with a Kenwood system built around what was then a genuine novelty: a head unit that could read MP3 discs. It made 140 horsepower. Mazda planned 1,000 and built 1,500 — the first thousand in Laser Blue Mica, the last five hundred in Vivid Yellow.

Here is the detail that matters for this article. Much of the MP3's body kit was not invented for it. The chin spoiler, the skirts, the fog lamps came off the Japanese-market Familia Sport 20 — which is to say, off the car Americans would later buy as the Protegé5. The MP3 was wearing the wagon's clothes a year before the wagon showed up.

Then came the Protegé5 itself for 2002, and it did something the MP3 never managed: it made all of that available to normal people at a normal price, with a hatch on the back. Base price, $16,815. It was not a limited edition. You could just go and buy one.

And then, for 2003, Mazda's newly minted in-house tuning arm produced the Mazdaspeed Protegé — the sequel with fangs. A Garrett T25 turbocharger developed with help from Callaway, 170 horsepower and 160 lb-ft, a Tochigi Fuji limited-slip differential, fatter 24 mm driveshafts, a heavy-duty clutch, bigger brakes, Bridgestone Potenza RE040s on new Racing Harts, and a Sparco-and-Nardi interior. Mazda built roughly 4,500 of them across the initial black-and-orange cars and the mid-year "2003.5" run.

Sedan, sedan, hatch. Warm, hot, and useful. The Protegé5 is the middle of that sandwich, and like a lot of middle children it got less attention than either sibling while quietly being the easiest one to live with.

All three share the same 2.0-liter FS four. The MP3 got 10 more from calibration; the Mazdaspeed got 30 more from a turbocharger. Only one of the three has a hatchback.

What it does on a road

Somewhere around 2,750 pounds — Edmunds weighed a test car at 2,716, Car and Driver weighed a better-equipped one at 2,810 — and yet the responses belong to something lighter still. Ask the Protegé5 to change direction and it has already done it, with a crispness that current compact hatchbacks, several generations more sophisticated, mostly cannot produce. The reason is not exotic. A hydraulic rack with restrained assistance, a slim wheel rim, and a shell rigid enough that the message from the contact patch does not get diluted somewhere between the tire and your palms.

That last point deserves a moment, because it explains a preference that sounds like snobbery and isn't. A steering wheel is a filter. Wrap the rim in enough foam and leather and you get something that feels reassuringly substantial in a showroom and arrives at your palms having quietly deleted half of what the front axle was trying to say. The Protegé5's rim is slim and barely padded, which looks like a cost saving and functions as an engineering decision. Put a period MINI beside it — a car with every reason on paper to be the Mazda's equal for agility and chatter — and the Mazda is simply telling you more.

The balance underneath is friendly rather than knife-edged. Ease out of the throttle on the way into a bend and the back axle will step around a few useful degrees, enough to tighten your line and no further. Stay in it and the car stays where you pointed it. Stability control was never on the options sheet, and the Protegé5 does not need it to be safe — it needs you to be paying attention, which is a different and more enjoyable requirement. On a wet surface or a snow-covered lot, provoking anything genuinely untidy takes real determination.

The Protegé5 never asks you to forgive its 130 horsepower. It asks you to use all of them.

The brakes are the underrated part. In that Edmunds six-car test, the Protegé5 was the only entry to stop from 60 mph in under 130 feet — 123 feet, ahead of a PT Cruiser at 130, a Matrix at 131, and a Focus at 133. It was also the quickest through the 600-foot slalom at 65.3 mph. Neither number is what you expect from a $17,000 wagon with 130 horsepower.

The greenhouse

Then there is the visibility, which in 2026 reads as science fiction. Glass everywhere, pillars like pencils, a cowl that stops well below your sightline. Blind spots are basically a design compromise the Protegé5 declined to make — the mirrors are close to a formality, because turning your head actually shows you something. You sit high enough over that low dash to know precisely where the front corners are when you thread a gap, and low enough beneath the header that the top of the windshield isn't cropping the road ahead into a letterbox.

Nothing on sale now offers that combination at any price. A showroom's nearest answer is a crossover, which hands you the ride height and then plants a deep, slab-fronted dashboard between you and the pavement. You get the elevation without the sightlines, which is the wrong half of the bargain.

The gripes are small and familiar. Anyone who has spent real time in an NA or NB Miata will recognize the first: the cushion rides an inch or two higher than it should, and there is no adjustment left to claw it back. The second is the seat itself, which is a decent piece of furniture — comfortable well beyond what $17,000 was buying in 2002 — that writes a check its bolsters cannot cash. It is shaped like something that will hold you through a quick corner. It won't. Edmunds' editors placed the front seats fourth of six for comfort and the ride quality mid-pack, and neither verdict is unfair.

The shape, which was the point

Mazda did not simply saw the trunk off a Protegé sedan. The Protegé5 is actually shorter than the sedan — 170.5 inches against 175.3 — because the rear overhang was cut back rather than stretched out. That is the opposite of how wagons are normally made, and it is why the proportions land: cropped tail, long roof, wheels shoved out to the corners. Practically speaking you are buying the roofline and the hatch, not the extra length a wagon badge usually promises. It looks like something with a considerably larger price on the window.

The rear quarter is where the design earns its money. Turning a three-box sedan into a five-door usually leaves visible evidence of the surgery, and here there is none — the junction where roof, hatch and rear fender all have to agree has been worked until it reads as the original intent rather than a conversion. The factory body kit and roof rails settle the car's attitude in exactly the right place: assertive without raising its voice.

Edmunds' editors, evaluating six compact wagons in early 2003, scored the Protegé5's exterior design a flat 10.0 out of 10. Nothing else in the test cleared 7.3. That is not a close call; that is a landslide.

Nobody is going to tell you the cabin feels expensive, because it doesn't. What it has instead is the rarer virtue of not lying about it. No fake stitching, no plastic doing an impression of brushed aluminum, no attempt to signal a price the car never charged. The materials are what a $17,000 budget bought in 2002, and Mazda put the money where a driver's hands and elbows actually land: padding where you lean, simplicity where you reach, everything a short move from the wheel. Two decades on, the perforated trim theme, the fat physical tuner knob and the leaned-back italic gauge lettering have aged into something you could reasonably call classic. It has more personality than most interiors built since, and it manages that without a single screen.

The engine, which is the honest problem

Nobody buys a Protegé5 for the engine, and nobody ever did.

The 2.0-liter FS is a narrow instrument. Ask it for anything below 2,000 rpm and it objects — booming, shuddering, audibly doing work it would rather not do. Take it past 4,000 and the pull simply goes flat; the claimed peak of 130 horsepower is filed at 6,000 rpm, but there is no moment behind the wheel where you feel it turn up. What is left is the middle two thousand revs, and the middle two thousand revs are genuinely good: clean, willing, with more texture than a spec sheet full of round numbers has any right to deliver. That happens to be precisely the band you live in on the roads this car was built for.

The Protegé5's entire personality lives in a 2,000 rpm window. Learn where it is and the car never feels slow.

The gear ratios make the same argument a second time. Fifth is short enough that 70 mph has the crank turning somewhere around 3,500 rpm, which produces the strange outcome of a car that drinks marginally more on the interstate than it does running errands across town. It also explains the one wish that has never left a Protegé5 forum in twenty-odd years: somebody, please, add a sixth. Consumption settles in the mid-20s at first and creeps into the high 20s once the engine has loosened up, and a genuinely restrained tank will break 30. The EPA filed it at 22 city and 28 highway.

What that gearing tells you is what the car is for. This is not a long-hauler. It is not the thing you point down an interstate for six hours. It is a two-hour drive with twists, bends, dips and backroads — a scenic route with corners in it, or a city you have to actually thread rather than cruise. On that road, the short gearing is a feature. On I-5, it is a drone.

What it was up against

The early 2000s were the last great age of the cheap, interesting five-door, and the Protegé5 landed in the middle of the crowd. Ford had just introduced the Focus ZX5. Toyota and Pontiac had the Matrix and Vibe. Chrysler had the PT Cruiser, which people were still paying over sticker for. Subaru had the Impreza TS and Outback Sport wagons, with the WRX above them. Suzuki had the Aerio SX. Honda's new Civic Si hatch was coming, and Acura's RSX Type-S sat a rung up.

In February 2003, Edmunds put six of them together — Matrix XR, PT Cruiser Limited, Protegé5, Focus ZX5, Impreza Outback Sport and Aerio SX — and the result is the single most revealing thing ever written about this car.

Now look at how it got there, because the Protegé5 did not finish second by being competent. It finished second by being extraordinary at half the job and last at the other half.

Feature content, scored separately, was dead last of six at 23.3 percent — no traction control, no stability control, no telescoping wheel, ABS optional.

And then the stat that should be printed on the sun visor of every Protegé5 still running. Edmunds asked its editors two questions at the end of the test. Which would you buy with your own money? Which would you recommend to an average shopper?

The Protegé5 scored 88.9 on the first question — the highest in the test by a wide margin, with the Matrix on 66.7. On the second question the Matrix scored a perfect 100 and the Protegé5 managed 55.6.

The people who tested them wanted the Mazda. They recommended the Toyota. Twenty-three years later, only one of those two answers looks like it aged well.

A smaller moment from the same test makes the point faster. Out on the drive loop, one of the editors found himself on a twisting road with a Subaru WRX filling his mirrors — a car holding an enormous power advantage and no room to spend it. The Mazda stayed in front anyway. When the two finally drew level at a light, the Subaru's driver leaned across to ask what he had been chasing; he had misread the badge and assumed Mazda was selling some hotter "Protegé S" that had escaped his attention. That exchange is the Protegé5's entire career in miniature — routinely mistaken for something quicker by the people who had just failed to catch it.

Car and Driver came away from its Supertuner Challenge that year with a version of the same story. A Protegé5 had been brought along as a general dogsbody, shuttling staff between stops, and on one leg it emerged that nobody aboard actually knew the route. The only way to reach the next location was to stay welded to the car ahead — which happened to be a twin-turbocharged Lingenfelter Corvette running 650 horsepower with the rubber and suspension to match. On Michigan back roads the Corvette could sensibly use only a fraction of that. The Mazda had no fraction in reserve; it was being wrung out completely, and it never lost contact. The magazine's own conclusion was that the man in the small hatchback was having the better afternoon of the two.

It raced, too

The Protegé's competition record is better than its reputation. In the 2002 SCCA Speed World Challenge Touring Car season, Mazda Protegés won at Road America in July with Paul Bonaccorsi and at Trois-Rivières in August with Chuck Hemmingson, in a class otherwise dominated by Acura Integra Type Rs and BMW 3 Series.

Why nobody sells one of these anymore

So why has the industry stopped offering this car in North America? There is no single villain, which is exactly the problem.

Visibility went first, and it went for two reasons at once. Roof-crush and side-impact standards made pillars thicker, and styling trends made beltlines higher and glass shallower. One of those was mandatory. The other was fashion. Together they turned the airy, thin-pillared greenhouse into something the market no longer builds at any price.

The chassis story is more complicated. The move to electric power-assisted steering, made for fuel-economy reasons, has not helped feel — but the honest version is that even cars retaining hydraulic assist have been delivering less and less of it for years, because the whole structure around the rack changed. More sound deadening, more isolation, more mass. Safety structure, airbags, electronics, actuators and driver-assistance hardware all cost weight, and weight is the enemy of the specific sensation this car is good at.

And the market itself changed. Cars no longer have to sell engagement, because engagement is no longer what most people are buying. More and more people want less involvement, not more — a machine that gets them where they are going with the least hassle and the least responsibility. Self-driving is the logical end of that, and it is worth saying plainly that the appeal is real. Getting into a Waymo and having it take you somewhere does have something to recommend it. You relax. You decompress. You actually see the landscape or the city going past, instead of the bumper in front of you.

In a word, the reason is refinement. Which sounds like a compliment and mostly is one. Modern cars are quieter, safer, faster, cleaner and more comfortable than a Protegé5 by every measurable standard, and anyone claiming otherwise is selling nostalgia. But refinement is subtractive as well as additive. Every layer of isolation that keeps the road out of the cabin also keeps the road out of your hands. The Protegé5 has almost none of those layers, which is why it is loud, why it is firm, why owners complain about wind noise at 70 — and why it is still one of the most alive things you can drive.

The Protegé5 delivers a visceral connection not only to the road, but to an age when driving a car meant becoming an extension of it.

The car it was quietly rehearsing for

Here is where the Protegé5 stops being a curiosity and starts being a link in a chain.

The Protegé was the last car Mazda sold in America under the Familia bloodline that ran back to 1963. It was replaced for 2004 by the Mazda3. Two years after that, Mazda took the Mazda3's platform, raised the roof, added a third row and a pair of sliding doors, and sold it here as the Mazda5.

So the Protegé5 and the Mazda5 are not just similarly named. They are the same idea two rounds apart, on the same architectural bloodline, aimed at the same buyer: someone who wants a car-sized car that can be asked to do more than a car normally does, and who does not want to be punished for it on a good road. The Protegé5 hid the utility inside a shape that looked like a European sport wagon. The Mazda5 stopped hiding it and put doors on the side. Both were praised. Both were outsold by taller, duller things. Both are now cheap.

The difference is what the two cars were missing. The Mazda5's problem was timing — America wasn't ready for a small van, and by the time it was, the Mazda5 was gone. The Protegé5's problem was more specific and more fixable: about 30 horsepower and a sixth gear. Mazda knew it, too. That is precisely what the Mazdaspeed Protegé added, one model year later, to a sedan.

The wagon Mazda never built

There was never a Mazdaspeed Protegé5. The turbocharged drivetrain, the limited-slip differential and the bigger brakes all went into the four-door only, and by the time the Mazdaspeed program hit its stride the whole Protegé line was a year from retirement.

This is why a meaningful number of Protegé5s on the road today are running Mazdaspeed or MP3 hardware. The community built the car Mazda didn't. Parts interchange almost completely.

What they cost now

This is the part where the Protegé5 stops being a nice memory and becomes an actionable idea, because the gap between what the books say and what the cars actually sell for is enormous.

Cheapest recent P5 auction sale$4,078

Sources: Kelley Blue Book, Cars.com, Edmunds and Classic.com listings and results, checked August 2026. Classic.com's average across all Protegé sales sits at $8,368, skewed upward by the Mazdaspeed cars.

Read that chart from the top and the story is obvious. The valuation books still treat a Protegé5 as an old economy car worth about fifteen hundred dollars. The actual market has decided otherwise and is paying four to seven thousand for good ones. That is not a bubble; that is a correction, and it is the same pattern every enthusiast car follows about five years before it stops being cheap.

The Mazdaspeed sedans are further along the same curve, and their spread is instructive: a modified example with 107,000 miles brought $4,600 at auction this summer, while a 59,000-mile original car made $7,350 last fall and a dealer is currently asking $19,500 for a 100,000-mile car. That $15,000 gap between a rough one and an optimistic asking price is the sound of a market that has not settled yet.

The practical read: a sorted, rust-free, manual Protegé5 is a $5,000–$7,000 car today. That is roughly one month of payments on the average new vehicle.

Why you'd actually buy one

Four cases, and they are all real.

As a track car or an autocross car. The chassis is already better than the engine, which is the correct problem to have. Modify it and it keeps pace: MP3 or Mazdaspeed springs and dampers, a set of proper tires, the well-known fixes for the rear sway bar mounts. Where a modern hot hatch gives you 300 horsepower and asks $40,000, this gives you a talkative chassis and asks for a weekend and a credit card that has seen worse.

As the second car while the EV charges. This is a genuinely modern use case and the Protegé5 is unusually good at it. Small footprint, easy to park, cheap to insure, cheap to fix, carries a bicycle or a hardware run, and turns a dull errand into something you'd volunteer for. It also asks nothing of you when it sits — no battery anxiety, no software updates, no subscription.

As a first car for your kid. Slow enough that it cannot get them into serious trouble, engaging enough that they will actually learn to drive rather than learn to steer, cheap enough that a scraped bumper is a shrug, and manual if you want it to be — which remains the single best way to occupy a new driver's hands and attention. The safety caveat is real and worth saying out loud: this is a car from 2002 with two airbags, optional ABS and no stability control. It is not a modern car in a crash. Weigh that honestly.

As the cheapest ticket to something that is disappearing. There is no new car at any price that offers this combination of thin pillars, thin steering wheel rim, low mass and hydraulic feel. Not one. You cannot order it. You can only buy a used one, and the supply is finite and rusting.

What to look at before you hand over money

The Protegé5 is a simple, robust car with a short and well-known list of failings. Check these and you will avoid almost every bad one.

Rust, first and above everything. These corrode with real enthusiasm, particularly the rear wheel arches and the area around the fuel tank. A salt-belt car with bubbling arches is a project, not a purchase. Buy a southern or western car if you possibly can.

The rear subframe and sway bar mounts. A clunk from the back over bumps is the signature complaint. The end links bind and break and the rear bar's mounting to the subframe is a weak design. Both are known quantities with known fixes; just price them in.

Rear calipers. They seize. Feel for uneven pad wear and a warm wheel after a drive.

Ignition coils and plug wires. Failure-prone, cheap, and sitting right on top of the engine. A misfire left alone will take out the catalytic converter, which is the only expensive thing on this list. Replace them preemptively.

Timing belt. Roughly a 100,000-mile item, and documentation matters. You will find people insisting the FS is an interference engine and people insisting it isn't; the Gates catalog and most Mazda technicians say non-interference, but the disagreement is old and heated enough that the sensible move is to treat it as if a failure would be catastrophic and simply change it on schedule.

Don't hang it at the redline mid-corner. The FS's oiling is the powertrain's known limitation, and the failure mode enthusiasts report is a rod bearing. It is not a fragile engine in normal use — plenty of these have passed 200,000 miles — but it is not a race engine either, and it does not enjoy being held against the limiter while loaded up in a long turn.

The verdict

The Protegé5 was never the best car in any comparison test and it was never going to be. It lost on features, it lost on power, it lost on refinement, and it lost to a Toyota that did everything adequately. What it won was the only category that survives twenty-three years: the editors who drove all six wanted this one for themselves.

That is still the correct answer. Everything the Protegé5 was penalized for in 2003 — the missing content, the loud cabin, the firm ride, the modest engine — turns out to be the price of the things nobody sells anymore. And everything it won on then, it still wins on now, against cars built two decades later.

It is the happy medium in every sense. Between the MP3 and the Mazdaspeed. Between fun and useful. Between a car you enjoy and a car you can justify. Five thousand dollars, a clean underside, and a road with some bends in it — and it will still answer the way it always did.

Sounds awesome.
